title: Operating System — Part 1: Process Management & CPU Scheduling
subtitle: Exam-level practice on process states, schedulers, PCB, context switching, CPU scheduling, starvation, semaphores and spooling.
source: Original exam-style question bank based on the user-provided sample questions and the linked video’s process-management / CPU-scheduling scope. Numerical answers independently checked.
instructions: Choose one answer for each question.
25 questions · 1 mark each · no negative marking.
Review the explanation, important point, exam trap and hint after answering.
description: Process states, PCB, schedulers, context switching, FCFS/SJF/SRTF/Round Robin, waiting-time calculations, starvation, semaphores and spooling.

questions.question: A process has completed execution, but its process-table entry remains because the parent has not yet collected its exit status. Which state best describes it?
questions.explanation: The process has terminated, but the kernel retains its process-table entry until the parent collects its status (for example, with wait()).
questions.importantPoint: A zombie has exited but still has an unreaped process-table entry.
questions.examTrap: An orphan is still executing after its parent terminates; a zombie has already exited.
questions.hint: Focus on whether the process has finished executing or is still running.

questions.question: A parent process terminates while its child continues executing. The child is best described as:
questions.explanation: A child that continues after its parent exits is an orphan; it may be adopted by a system process.
questions.importantPoint: Orphan describes the parent-child lifetime relationship.
questions.examTrap: A zombie is terminated; an orphan is still running or otherwise alive.
questions.hint: Determine whether the child has terminated.

questions.question: Which transition is invalid in the standard five-state process model, assuming no special direct-dispatch mechanism?
questions.explanation: A blocked process must first become ready when the awaited event completes; it does not normally move directly from blocked to running.
questions.importantPoint: Event completion moves Blocked → Ready; dispatch moves Ready → Running.
questions.examTrap: Do not confuse becoming eligible to run with actually receiving the CPU.
questions.hint: Separate the event-completion transition from the scheduler-dispatch transition.

questions.question: Which scheduler primarily controls the degree of multiprogramming by deciding which jobs are admitted into main memory?
questions.explanation: The long-term (job) scheduler admits jobs into the system and influences how many processes are in memory.
questions.importantPoint: Long-term scheduling controls admission and degree of multiprogramming.
questions.examTrap: The short-term scheduler selects a ready process for the CPU; the dispatcher performs the handoff.
questions.hint: Ask which component controls admission into the ready pool.

questions.question: A system temporarily swaps a suspended process out of main memory and later brings it back. Which scheduler is most directly associated with this medium-term activity?
questions.explanation: The medium-term scheduler manages swapping/suspension to adjust the set of processes resident in memory.
questions.importantPoint: Medium-term scheduling is associated with swapping and suspended states.
questions.examTrap: Do not confuse swapping with selecting the next CPU-bound process.
questions.hint: Look for the scheduler associated with temporarily removing processes from memory.

questions.question: Which item is normally stored in a Process Control Block (PCB) to allow a process to resume correctly after a context switch?

options.text: Saved program counter and CPU registers
The complete contents of every file opened by the process

questions.explanation: The PCB stores execution context such as process state, program counter, registers, scheduling information and memory-management information.
questions.importantPoint: A PCB stores process-management and saved execution-context information.
questions.examTrap: Open-file references may be managed in kernel structures, but the source code itself is not the saved CPU context.
questions.hint: Which information is needed to continue execution at the correct instruction?

questions.question: A timer interrupt causes the running process to be preempted, and the scheduler chooses another ready process. Which operation saves the old execution context and restores the new one?
questions.explanation: A context switch saves the outgoing process/thread state and restores the selected one.
questions.importantPoint: Context switching changes the CPU execution context.
questions.examTrap: A timer interrupt may trigger scheduling, but the interrupt itself is not the context switch.
questions.hint: Think about what must happen before a different process can safely resume.

questions.question: Consider two processes: P1 arrives at time 0 with burst 7; P2 arrives at time 2 with burst 3. Under non-preemptive SJF, what is the completion order?
questions.explanation: At time 0 only P1 is available, so non-preemptive SJF runs P1 until time 7. P2 then runs and finishes at time 10.
questions.importantPoint: Non-preemptive SJF does not interrupt the running job when a shorter job arrives.
questions.examTrap: Do not apply SRTF rules to non-preemptive SJF.
questions.hint: At time zero, which jobs have actually arrived?

questions.question: Processes arrive as follows: P1 (AT=0, BT=8), P2 (AT=1, BT=4), P3 (AT=2, BT=2). Using SRTF and breaking ties by earlier arrival, which is the Gantt-chart sequence?
questions.explanation: At t=1, P2 has 4 versus P1 remaining 7; at t=2, P3 has 2 versus P2 remaining 3. P3 completes at 4, P2 at 7, and P1 at 14.
questions.importantPoint: SRTF always selects the available process with the shortest remaining time.
questions.examTrap: Compare remaining time, not original burst time, at each arrival.
questions.hint: Re-evaluate the ready set at t=1 and again at t=2.

questions.question: For the processes in Q9, what is the average waiting time under SRTF?
questions.explanation: Completion times are P3=4, P2=7, P1=14. Waiting time = CT−AT−BT: P1=14−0−8=6, P2=7−1−4=2, P3=4−2−2=0. Average = (6+2+0)/3 = 8/3 ≈ 2.67.
questions.importantPoint: Waiting time = completion time − arrival time − burst time.
questions.examTrap: Turnaround time is not the same as waiting time.
questions.hint: Calculate each process waiting time separately, then average.

questions.question: Three processes all arrive at time 0: P1 BT=5, P2 BT=3, P3 BT=1. Under non-preemptive SJF, what is the average waiting time?
questions.explanation: Order is P3 (0–1), P2 (1–4), P1 (4–9). Waiting times are 0, 1 and 4; average = 5/3 ≈ 1.67.
questions.importantPoint: SJF minimizes average waiting time when all jobs are available and burst lengths are known.
questions.examTrap: The first process in the SJF order waits zero time.
questions.hint: Order by burst time and calculate each start time minus arrival time.

questions.question: In Round Robin, P1, P2 and P3 arrive at time 0 with burst times 5, 4 and 2 respectively. With quantum=2 and no context-switch overhead, when does P2 complete?
questions.explanation: Execution: P1 0–2, P2 2–4, P3 4–6 (finishes), P1 6–8 (remaining 1), P2 8–10 (finishes), P1 10–11. P2 completes at time 10.
questions.importantPoint: Round Robin requeues unfinished processes at the tail after their quantum.
questions.examTrap: Do not forget processes that finish before using the full quantum.
questions.hint: Write the ready-queue rotation after each time slice.

questions.question: A Round Robin scheduler uses a very large time quantum compared with every process burst. Ignoring arrivals during execution, it approaches which policy?
questions.explanation: When the quantum is large enough that each process finishes before its quantum expires, the ready queue is served in arrival order, making RR behave like FCFS.
questions.importantPoint: A sufficiently large RR quantum makes preemption unlikely.
questions.examTrap: This does not make RR equivalent to SJF.
questions.hint: Ask whether any process is likely to exhaust the quantum before finishing.

questions.question: Which scheduling policy can cause starvation because newly arriving short jobs may repeatedly be selected ahead of a long job?
questions.explanation: SJF can indefinitely delay a long job if shorter jobs continue to arrive and are selected first.
questions.importantPoint: Starvation is indefinite postponement despite the process remaining eligible.
questions.examTrap: Aging is a technique used to reduce starvation in priority scheduling.
questions.hint: Consider what happens if short jobs keep arriving before the long job is selected.

questions.question: Priority scheduling is causing a low-priority process to wait for an unusually long time. Which change directly addresses this risk?

options.text: Increase the low-priority process’s waiting time in the queue
Use aging to gradually raise its priority
Replace every process with a new process

questions.explanation: Aging gradually increases a waiting process’s priority, reducing the chance of indefinite postponement.
questions.importantPoint: Aging combats starvation by changing effective priority over time.
questions.examTrap: Aging is not the same as increasing CPU burst length.
questions.hint: Choose the technique that rewards prolonged waiting.

questions.question: Which statement about preemptive scheduling is the most accurate?

options.text: It can preempt a running process when a scheduling event warrants it.
It always has lower context-switch overhead than non-preemptive scheduling.
It guarantees that starvation never occurs.

questions.explanation: Preemptive scheduling permits the OS to take the CPU from a running process under defined conditions, often after a timer interrupt or a higher-priority arrival.
questions.importantPoint: Preemption improves responsiveness but can add switching overhead.
questions.examTrap: Preemption alone does not guarantee fairness or prevent starvation.
questions.hint: Separate what preemption permits from what it guarantees.

questions.question: A process has AT=3, BT=5 and CT=14. What are its turnaround time and waiting time, respectively?
questions.explanation: Turnaround time = CT−AT = 14−3 = 11. Waiting time = TAT−BT = 11−5 = 6.
questions.importantPoint: TAT = CT−AT; WT = TAT−BT when no other service time is specified.
questions.examTrap: Completion time is not itself turnaround time if arrival is nonzero.
questions.hint: First subtract arrival from completion, then subtract burst.

questions.question: For a single CPU, which scheduling criterion most directly measures the time from a process’s arrival until it first receives CPU service?
questions.explanation: Response time is the interval from arrival/submission until the first response or first CPU service, depending on the stated convention.
questions.importantPoint: Response time focuses on the first response, not final completion.
questions.examTrap: Turnaround time measures arrival to completion.
questions.hint: The process need not finish for this metric to be measured.

questions.question: Which pair is correctly matched?

options.text: Long-term scheduler — selects the next ready process for CPU
Short-term scheduler — admits jobs from secondary storage into memory
Dispatcher — hands CPU control to the selected process

questions.explanation: The dispatcher performs the context switch and transfers control to the selected process. The other choices mix scheduler responsibilities or describe unrelated work.
questions.importantPoint: Scheduler selects; dispatcher hands over CPU control.
questions.examTrap: Do not interchange long-term admission and short-term CPU selection.
questions.hint: Look for the component responsible for the actual handoff.

questions.question: A process blocks for disk I/O while running. When the I/O completes, which transition normally occurs before it can execute again?
questions.explanation: Completion of the awaited I/O makes the process ready; it must still be dispatched before it runs.
questions.importantPoint: I/O completion makes a process eligible, not automatically the CPU owner.
questions.examTrap: The CPU may be executing another process when the I/O completes.
questions.hint: Distinguish becoming runnable from being selected.

questions.question: A counting semaphore starts at 6. Eight successful wait (P) operations and four successful signal (V) operations occur, with no blocked operations or other accesses. What is the final value?
questions.explanation: Each successful P decrements and each V increments: 6−8+4=2.
questions.importantPoint: A successful wait decrements; a signal increments.
questions.examTrap: If waits block, the simple arithmetic model must account for blocked operations; this question explicitly says all are successful.
questions.hint: Apply the operation counts with their signs.

questions.question: Two processes may update the same shared counter. Which requirement ensures that the critical section is not executed by both processes at the same time?
questions.explanation: Mutual exclusion allows at most one process at a time inside the critical section for the same protected resource.
questions.importantPoint: Mutual exclusion prevents simultaneous entry into a critical section.
questions.examTrap: Progress and bounded waiting address different correctness properties.
questions.hint: Identify the property that explicitly limits concurrent entrants.

questions.question: A print subsystem places output jobs in a disk-based queue so the printer can process them at its own speed while applications continue. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Spooling queues jobs, commonly on disk, for a device such as a printer that processes them sequentially.
questions.importantPoint: Spooling decouples application submission from slower device execution.
questions.examTrap: Paging and swapping are memory-management mechanisms.
questions.hint: Focus on buffering queued jobs for a shared peripheral.

questions.question: Which statement about context switching is correct?

options.text: It always performs useful application work while the CPU changes processes.
It may add overhead because the CPU saves/restores execution state rather than executing application instructions.
It occurs only when a process terminates.
It is identical to switching from user mode to kernel mode.

questions.explanation: Saving and restoring context consumes CPU time and is generally overhead from the application-work perspective.
questions.importantPoint: Context switches are necessary but can reduce useful CPU time.
questions.examTrap: A mode switch does not necessarily imply a process context switch.
questions.hint: Ask whether the CPU is executing the process’s workload during the state transfer.

questions.question: Consider these statements: I. SRTF may starve a long process. II. Round Robin usually improves response time for interactive workloads compared with FCFS. III. A very large Round Robin quantum tends toward FCFS behavior. Which set is correct?
questions.explanation: SRTF can repeatedly favor short remaining jobs; RR gives processes periodic turns, improving responsiveness in many interactive workloads; with a sufficiently large quantum, RR approximates FCFS.
questions.importantPoint: Scheduling trade-offs depend on workload and quantum size.
questions.examTrap: “Usually” is intentional: RR does not universally outperform FCFS on every metric.
questions.hint: Evaluate each statement independently, noting the qualifier in II.
